description:
Cilantro, also called coriander (Coriandrum sativum), is a common kitchen herb. In North America, cilantro usually refers to the fresh leaves and stems, while coriander refers to the dried seeds; both come from the same plant. It is safe for cats. The ASPCA lists cilantro as non-toxic to cats, dogs and horses.

A cat that nibbles a few fresh leaves or tastes food seasoned with coriander does not need any treatment. Eating a large amount of the herb can cause mild, short-lived stomach upset such as vomiting or soft stool, simply because cats are not built to digest much plant material. Ground coriander seed is a mild spice and is not harmful in the small amounts found in cooked food.

Cilantro should not become a regular part of your cat's diet, but there is no need to worry about an occasional taste. Contact your veterinarian only if vomiting is repeated or your cat seems unwell.
name: Cilantro / Coriander
safetyNotes: Safe: Listed by the ASPCA as non-toxic to cats; leaves, stems and seeds contain no known poisonous compounds.
Possible reaction: Eating a large amount of leaves may cause mild, brief vomiting or soft stool, as with any plant material.
Watch for: Seasoned dishes may also contain onion, garlic or chili, which are the real hazards.
Action: No treatment needed for a nibble; contact a vet only if vomiting repeats or your cat seems unwell.

symptoms.name: Mild vomiting or soft stool after eating a large amount
symptoms.notes: Not a toxic reaction; cats cannot digest large amounts of plant fibre. Resolves on its own.
symptoms.onset: Within a few hours of eating a large amount

treatments.name: No treatment needed
treatments.notes: Contact a vet only if vomiting is repeated or other signs appear.
